title: The Pharisee and the tax collector (Luke 18:9–14)
hookLine: one prays about his own virtues; the other stands far off and asks only for mercy

lines: TWO MEN GO UP TO PRAY.
cards: Two men walk up to the temple in Jerusalem to pray. The first is a Pharisee. He stands and prays about himself.
God, thank you that I'm not like other people. Not a cheat, not a crook, not unfaithful. Not like that tax collector back there.
I fast twice a week. I give a tenth of everything I get. The second man is that tax collector.
He won't come close. He stands far off, won't even lift his eyes, and beats his own chest. He says one sentence.

teach.h: A SERIOUS MAN, NOT A FAKE
teach.b: Be fair to the Pharisee first; the story only works if you are. Pharisees were serious about God's law, and respected for it. This man isn't a fake, and the story never says he's lying.

teach.h: A PRAYER WITH ONE EYE ON THE NEIGHBOR
teach.b: His fasting and giving are real devotion, and his prayer starts well, with thanks. Then it turns: "God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are." One eye on God, one eye on the man at the back.
The whole prayer is a comparison. Now the tax collector. Tax collectors gathered money for the rulers of the land, and the Pharisee's own prayer files this one next to extortioners.
His prayer in the old King James is seven words: "God be merciful to me a sinner." No list. No comparison.
Just the truth, said once. And Jesus says: "this man went down to his house justified rather than the other." Justified means made right.
Luke tells us who the story was for: people who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and looked down on everyone else. Not Pharisees. Anyone.
Which sets a trap: the moment you think, thank God I'm not like that Pharisee, you've prayed his prayer. The tax collector's line has had a long life.

teach.h: GOD BE MERCIFUL TO ME A SINNER.
teach.b: Orthodox Christians trace the Jesus Prayer to it: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner. Monks and grandmothers say it over and over, quietly, through the day.
Read this way, the story makes a quiet promise: an honest sentence is enough to bring.

how: Christians pray short, honest prayers in their own words, and Orthodox Christians often repeat the Jesus Prayer ("Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner"), which tradition traces to the tax collector's plea.

o: excused because you had a good reason
made right with God, declared in the clear
proved right after winning an argument

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: fasts twice a week, tithes it all
stands far off, beats his chest
grows from the tax collector's line

s: Pharisees were fakes everyone saw through
they were serious about God's law, and respected for it. the story only works because this one is truly devout.
the Pharisee's prayer begins with thanks
"God, I thank thee" — and then it turns into a comparison.
Luke says the story was aimed at Pharisees
Luke says it was told to anyone who trusted in themselves and looked down on others.

games.q: you're in the crowd. Jesus asks: which of the two men went home right with God?
o: the Pharisee: he kept the law, and more.
the tax collector: he told the truth.
games.why: "this man went down to his house justified rather than the other." the verdict goes to the man the other one looked down on.

practice: Let the day come up, then drop the list and the comparisons, and find one completely honest sentence: I'm tired, or I got that wrong, or thank you. If you pray, say it to God; if you don't, say it to the quiet.
Say it once, then sit with it, adding nothing.

wordCard.voice: Justified. Made right with God, the word Luke uses for the tax collector who went home that way, after praying one honest sentence.

orig.note: Greek: "be merciful." the heart of the tax collector's seven words.

carryVoice: Your line: honesty is the whole prayer. Seven words were enough for the tax collector. Thirty-two, and counting.
